results.title: Where to Rent an H100 SXM at the Cheapest Price (October 2026)
results.author: GPUBank Research
highlights:
A good part of the market moved in the three weeks before this page was written, and almost all of it moved up. Nebius raised its on-demand H100 from $3.85 to $4.50 on 1 October and switched its preemptible tier to a dynamic spot price from 8 October 2; AWS now charges $5.97 per accelerator-hour for P5 Capacity Blocks in every region it lists 7; Verda lists $4.17 8, Crusoe $4.50 9 and JarvisLabs $3.49 10, all above the figures of late September, and CUDO Compute, which trackers still show at $1.79, now answers 'Quote on request' on its own pricing page 11. GPUBank, which publishes this page, is one of the providers compared, on the same terms as the others: we say where it is cheapest and where a marketplace listing, a spot tier or a reservation elsewhere beats it.

...

The H100 SXM is NVIDIA's Hopper datacenter GPU in its mezzanine form: 80 GB of HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s, NVLink at 900 GB/s between the GPUs of one server against 128 GB/s over PCIe Gen5, the FP8 Transformer Engine, 3,958 teraFLOPS of FP8 and 1,979 teraFLOPS of FP16 with sparsity, and a configurable power limit of up to 700 W 12. The module does not plug into a PCIe slot. It sits on an HGX baseboard of eight GPUs inside a complete server, which is why the 8-GPU node, not the single card, is the unit in which the H100 SXM is built, bought and very often rented.

...

Beyond the six providers profiled in detail, the managed tier is crowded and has mostly moved up. Voltage Park says on its own pricing page that one H100 can be rented for an hour from $1.99 without a contract, with no ingress, egress or support fees, while its Ethernet and InfiniBand configurations are priced on request 19. GetDeploying shows UpCloud at $1.89 an hour and $1.88 spot, both out of stock and without a stated variant 5. Hyperstack's H100 SXM page gives $3.20 on demand and reservations from $2.72, under a banner saying the card is only available through its Supercloud reservation, so treat the on-demand figure as a list price rather than a machine you can start today 20. JarvisLabs charges $3.49 per minute-billed hour with 16 vCPU and 200 GB of RAM 10, Verda $4.17 with 30 vCPU and 120 GB 8, DigitalOcean $4.41 with 20 vCPU, 240 GiB, 5 TiB of scratch NVMe and 15,000 GiB of transfer 17, and Crusoe and Nebius both $4.50 9 2.

results.title: Compute market report — 2026-10-11 | Price of Compute
Where to rent an A100 SXM at the cheapest price - GPUBank
results.author: GPUBank Research
highlights:
Cheap per hour is not the same as cheap per job, and the measured ratios decide which card to rent. On GPUBank the H100 SXM costs 1.95 times the A100's rate, so the A100 stays the sensible choice wherever the H100 is less than about twice as fast: long-sequence and memory-bound inference, ResNet-style training, BF16 stacks that cannot use FP8, QLoRA runs that spend real time loading data and writing checkpoints, notebooks that sit idle, and any session billed while you think. The H100 is cheaper per job on short, compute-heavy work and on anything that can run FP8, as the BERT result shows, and its advantage grows with concurrency. The practical test costs little: run your own job for half an hour on each card at per-second rates, divide the price by the throughput you measured, and keep the cheaper card.

...

A managed cloud sells a fixed machine, the GPU with its vCPUs, memory and local disk, at one hourly price that may or may not include the public IP, the persistent storage and the traffic. For the A100 SXM that group runs from GPUBank's $0.95 through CloudRift at $1.05, Thunder Compute at $1.09, Beam at $1.36, Massed Compute at $1.38, Jarvislabs at $1.49 and Hyperstack at $1.60 to Runpod Secure Cloud at $1.79 and Verda at $1.996 1 2 3 16 17 12 18 5 19. A peer-to-peer marketplace lets independent hosts post their own GPU price and bills storage and bandwidth as separate lines set by each host, which is why Vast.ai's $0.937 and a managed $0.95 are not two prices for the same product even though they sit a cent apart 4.

...

Beyond the six offers shown as cards, several managed clouds sell a single A100 80 GB at prices between $1.36 and $2.00. Beam lists an A100 80 GB SXM4 machine from $1.36 an hour with 16 vCPU, 128 GB of RAM and 1 TB of NVMe, one of the most generous machines in this price range 16. Jarvislabs charges $1.49 with 16 vCPU and 112 GB of RAM, billed per minute, without saying SXM or PCIe on its pricing page, and GetDeploying showed Geodd's A100 SXM with 16 vCPU and 120 GB and Sesterce's unlabelled A100 80 GB, both at $1.49 and in stock on 15 October 9; and Hyperstack lists its A100 SXM at $1.60 on demand and $1.36 reserved, with up to 24 pCPU and 120 GB of RAM, next to a PCIe A100 at $1.35 12 18. Verda, formerly DataCrunch, now shows $1.996 per GPU-hour for its A100 SXM4 80 GB in one, two, four and eight-GPU sizes, up from the $1.79 we recorded at the end of September, with 22 CPUs and 120 GB of RAM listed against the card 19. Above that range, and only by the eight-GPU instance, Crusoe lists an A100 80 GB SXM at $2.30 per GPU-hour next to a PCIe version at $2.00, and Lambda sells its A100 SXM 80 GB as an eight-GPU instance at $2.79 per GPU with 240 vCPU, 1,800 GiB of RAM and 19.5 TiB of SSD 21 6.

The version. On-demand, the PCIe 80 GB starts at $1.99, the NVL 94 GB starts at $2.59 and the SXM 80 GB starts at $2.69. PCIe is a card that fits a standard server slot. It runs at lower power than SXM and links to other GPUs more slowly, and it is usually the cheaper version to rent. NVL is a PCIe card made to be paired with a second one over an NVLink bridge, so the two share data quickly. It draws less power than the SXM version. SXM is a module mounted on NVIDIA's HGX board, where GPUs share data over NVLink. It runs at full power with the fastest links between GPUs, which is why 8-GPU training machines use it.

results.title: Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun - DEV Community
results.author: Paul Piper
highlights:
Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun - DEV Community
Paul Piper
Posted on Oct 20 • Originally published at madppiper.substack.com
# Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun
Part of my job, and honestly part of my hobby, is watching prices. Not all of them, of course (I mean, what a lunatic must you be), but specific ones: GPU and inference endpoints. A while back I noticed that they differ immensely across providers, so I built a tool. Smart Inference, the router Jenni and I run, reads the price of GPU rentals and LLM tokens from a list of providers around the clock and sends each request to the cheapest healthy option. Since April it has kept every price it ever saw, which by now is roughly 11 million GPU price points and 3.3 million token prices.
I was wondering if my own data would support my theory that there is “overcapacity in the market”. Alas, that is not really what it shows.
I start in June, because before that we had too few providers to say much. From June to October, the median hourly price of the GPUs everybody wants went up:
* H100, on-demand: 3.25 to 3.89 dollars (+20%)
* H200, on-demand: 4.00 to 5.02 dollars (+25%)
* B200, on-demand: 6.11 to 7.42 dollars (+21%)
* B200, spot: 2.14 to 3.78 dollars (+77%)
Meanwhile, even the spot pricing options jumped: H100 in June was offered at a low of 1.04 an hour, and was bumped to 1.81 in October. This fits the overall market trend.
There is one exception, however and that is older hardware: An A100 on spot went from 1.07 to 0.88 an hour back in July and has sat there ever since. So it looks like people are fighting over newer hardware and perhaps if you want to really make a bargain right now, those can be a better choice.
Then I looked at the token side (my inference endpoints) and that’s where it got weird: Across all providers that serve the same model, the median price per million input tokens shifted a lot. DeepSeek V4 was at 1.30 dollars until July and is selling for 0.30 now, about 77% less. GLM-5 went from 1.00 in May to 0.15 in October. Output tokens fell almost as hard (DeepSeek V4: 2.60 down to 1.20, GLM-5: 3.20 to 0.50).
So a steep price drop, even though the models are unchanged and hardware got more expensive. To be fair, not everything got cheaper. Kimi K2.6 and GLM-4.7 stayed roughly the same, and gpt-oss-120b even went up a little at the median. But the big new open models, the ones people actually switch to, lost three quarters of their price or more within a few months of launch.
All in all, hardware got about 20% more expensive and inference got 80% cheaper. Makes no sense, but okay…
I have some theories why that may be: sometimes models are subsidized, other times providers get better at running the models (quantization is a thing) and maybe, just maybe older models are downgraded to lower specs (which could also have an impact on performance).
Theories aside, what it shows, however, is that my own idea that “the market is producing vast overcapacity for AI” is not really the case. At least not according to the data. If that were the case, my own pricing table, which also features “spot pricing”, should get cheaper over time, not more expensive. For current hardware it looks more like the opposite, the GPUs get pricier. It also means that sometimes model providers are eating the costs.
That matters more than you may think: it means that at least for now, it is more expensive to run your own GPU than it is to build on inference infrastructure. If token prices drop faster than GPU prices, renting your own GPU stops making sense for most workloads, and buying tokens from whoever is cheapest this week wins.
